old_row.relationship: Warning not to ascend without divine presence
old_row.rationale: The Lord’s warning through Moses prohibits ascent and predicts defeat because He is not among them; Numbers gives Moses’ corresponding warning, naming Amalek and the Canaanites as the opponents.

new_row.relationship: Warning not to ascend without divine presence
new_row.rationale: Both prohibit ascent without the Lord's presence; Deuteronomy says not to ascend and not be crushed, while Numbers explicitly predicts falling before the enemies and names Amalek and the Canaanites.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter explicit analogy of displaced inhabitants
old_row.rationale: The Lord’s removal of the powerful earlier inhabitants before Ammon’s descendants is followed by the explicit comparison with His removal of the Horites before Esau’s descendants in Seir. The analogy preserves separate peoples and territories.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter explicit analogy of displaced inhabitants
new_row.rationale: The Lord's destruction of the powerful earlier inhabitants before Ammon's descendants is followed by an explicit comparison with the Horites' displacement before Esau's descendants in Seir. The differing grammatical agents, peoples and territories remain distinct.

old_row.relationship: Sihon’s destruction explicitly used as Og comparison
old_row.rationale: The capture and destruction of Sihon’s towns includes men, women, and children; the Og recital expressly says his towns were destroyed as Sihon’s, likewise specifying men, women, and children.

new_row.relationship: Sihon’s destruction explicitly used as Og comparison
new_row.rationale: The capture and utter destruction of Sihon's towns explicitly names their women and children; the Og recital expressly compares its utter destruction of towns, with women and children, to Sihon's treatment.

old_row.relationship: Og brings his people to battle at Edrei
old_row.rationale: Both narratives describe the northward approach toward Bashan and Og king of Bashan coming out with all his people for battle at Edrei; these shared named particulars identify the narrated encounter.

new_row.relationship: Og brings his people to battle at Edrei
new_row.rationale: Both narratives describe turning onto the road toward Bashan and Og king of Bashan coming out with all his people for battle at Edrei; these shared named particulars identify the narrated encounter.

old_row.relationship: Explicit comparison with Sihon’s devoted towns
old_row.rationale: The Og campaign expressly follows the treatment of Sihon’s towns, destroying men, women, and children; the earlier recital records that treatment of the towns after the Lord delivered Sihon.

new_row.relationship: Explicit comparison with Sihon’s devoted towns
new_row.rationale: The Og campaign expressly compares its utter destruction of cities, with women and children, to Sihon's treatment; the earlier recital records the city's destruction and no captive left alive after Sihon's defeat.

old_row.relationship: Provoking adults excluded from the sworn land
old_row.rationale: The evil generation will not see the good land sworn to the fathers; Numbers likewise excludes the men who saw the signs yet repeatedly tested God from seeing that sworn land.

new_row.relationship: Provoking adults excluded from the sworn land
new_row.rationale: The excluded generation will not see the good land sworn to the fathers; Numbers likewise excludes the men who saw the signs yet repeatedly tested God from seeing that sworn land.
